lines.text: Here's a strange thing to build: an AI that isn't allowed to write. No sentences. No explanations. Just numbers. Why would anyone want that?
Most of us assume that more words means more understanding. A paragraph feels smarter than a number. But remember the train: every extra word was one more bet.

Jev starts with a contract. Before it reads anything, you fix the questions, and every answer it's allowed to give. Is this a scam: yes or no. Which team: billing, fraud, or lost card. How urgent: anywhere from zero to one. Those are the only signals it will ever be able to raise.
Picture a mailroom with a fixed wall of slots. A letter comes in. Jev reads the whole thing in a single sweep, and drops it into a slot.
Our train wants to help. It starts building a brand new slot. Miscellaneous-ish. But the wall has no room for it. Jev can pick the wrong slot. It can never invent a new one.
And it answers every question at once. Scam, team and urgency all come out of the same single reading, side by side, instead of one word after another.
Written as math, it's a product again. The chance of all three answers is the chance of each one, multiplied. The same symbol as the chain rule. But here, no answer has to wait for the one before it.
Now a harder letter. My card was charged twice, and now I can't find it. Is that billing, fraud, or a lost card? Make your pick.

Think of Jev's certainty as a hundred grains of light, poured into the answers. All of them in one, and it's sure. Spread evenly, and it has no idea. For this letter: forty seven go to fraud, twenty eight to billing, twenty five to lost card.
And that spread is useful. When no answer fills past a line, Jev doesn't have to bluff. You draw the line, and anything below it goes to a person.
But all of this rests on one promise. When Jev says ninety one percent, is it right about ninety one percent of the time? That promise has a name. And it's where we go next.
